Construct the reionization E template as Cℓ^EE(τ=0.06)−exp(−0.12)Cℓ^EE(τ=0), setting its small contribution above ℓ=20 to zero. Foreground-residual forecasts add adopted post-component-separation residual power to spectra entering the covariance.

Rotate each epoch's Stokes contribution by exp(±2iθx), sum the contributions, and transform with spin-2 spherical harmonics. For small angles, the stated EB template is Cℓ^(EB′)≈2Σx θx[Cℓ^(EE,x)−Cℓ^(BB,x)].

Higgs specializations relate partition functions; modular bootstrap in weak Jacobi forms fixes base-degree-one expressions. Genus-zero free energies fix normalizations, while modular results fix ambiguities in the genus-one ansatz.

Mirror periods and Picard-Fuchs equations determine monodromies and transfer matrices. Coordinate changes resolve tangencies between discriminants and the large-base boundary; numerical analytic continuation supplies transfer data where closed period expressions are unavailable.

Determine effective-cone chambers and wall types from intersection data and line-bundle cohomology. The tabulations use the CICY package for complete intersections and CohomCalg with SAGE for toric hypersurfaces.

Separate volume and shape geodesics. For h^{1,1}=2, solve the constant-volume constraint together with the conserved-energy equation; transform normal-form solutions back and match positions and velocities across flops.

Classify binary cubic intersection forms under GL(2,R), using the rank of the contraction map from symmetric tensors and the number of distinct real projective zeros. Map each physical cone into the positivity region of its normal form.

Select dominant monomials, solve a nonzero power-law balance, check omitted terms against the full vector field, and inspect the shifted Jacobian. The paper performs the balance and resonance stages, while the full-system dominance and physical-time conditions remain unresolved.

Study exceptions through circle reduction of five-dimensional Chern–Simons couplings, monopole/dyon estimates, and cubic-prepotential gauge kinetic matrices in two-field five-dimensional supergravity.
Analyze localized charged modes through modified magnetic Bianchi identities and a worldsheet democratic pseudo-action supplemented by self-duality constraints.
Combine the electric axion WGC, an assumed gauge-instanton action, and the WGC for the dual two-form to bound string tension. Apply anomaly inflow to relate axion strings to charged excitations.

Use the parametric conserved charges, largest-root horizon equation, area-law entropy and Gibbs energy G=M−TS−ΦQ−Ω_aJ_a−Ω_bJ_b. Eliminate q using Φ; retain auxiliary geometric parameters when inversion to intensive variables is impractical.

Expand potentials and G linearly around BPS values, impose two constraints defining a,b, and use homogeneity to construct intrinsic BPS thermodynamics. A Lagrange-multiplier formulation permits extremization over a,b before differentiating with respect to potentials.

Compare with the imported complex HHZ functional H=−N²Δ³/(2ω_aω_b), constrained by 3Δ−ω_a−ω_b=2πi. Constrained Legendre extremization and reality/positivity of entropy recover the entropy and charge constraint in the authors’ calculation.

Reviews amplitude matching in the Metsaev–Tseytlin approach and supersymmetry-based construction in the Bergshoeff–de Roo approach. Their comparison uses field redefinitions and torsionful spin connections w^(±)=w±H/2.

Uses generalized frames, complementary projectors, generalized Lie derivatives and fluxes to formulate DFT actions. Explicit parametrization and double-Lorentz gauge fixing connect doubled fields and transformations to ordinary supergravity fields.

Decomposes O(D,D+K) fields into O(D,D) multiplets, exposing a generalized gauge connection. Gauge generators map gauge indices to antisymmetric Lorentz pairs; identifying the connection with flux projections generates first-order corrections, followed by a proposed recursive extended-flux identification.

Couple higher-form symmetries to background fields using Stückelberg combinations. Express the action through an auxiliary X5 with boundary M4; changes of extension distinguish dynamical-field inconsistencies from background-only ’t Hooft anomalies.

Calculate symmetry transformations and intersection correlations by finite field reparameterizations, described as finite Schwinger–Dyson equations. Delta-form representatives, Stokes’ theorem and linking numbers track induced objects and fractional phases.

First-order dualization replaces the Stückelberg scalar by a 2-form BF description. Separating axion fluctuations from thin domain walls and introducing a 3-form multiplier dualizes the axion potential.

Reviewed background constructions use doubled coordinates and a generalized metric, homogeneous α′ corrections, and anisotropic external/internal scale factors. The matrix proposal instead takes N→∞ with g²N fixed and extracts time and spatial blocks from Hermitian matrices.

Thermal energy-density and off-diagonal stress correlations are connected to scalar and tensor perturbations through infrared linearized Einstein equations; the displayed matrix-model relations contain a 16π²G²k⁻⁴ factor.

Factor the anomaly transformation through σ:TMF→KO((q)), the fermion-anomaly map α_spin, and Anderson duality applied to the forgetful map from string to spin structure. A module-map lemma reduces the composite to one Anderson-dual class β_string.

The rational calculation uses vanishing of the constant coefficient of weakly holomorphic modular forms of weight two. The Anderson-dual Ext/Hom exact sequence and π_{−21}(TMF)=0 then make rationalization injective, eliminating the remaining integral ambiguity.

Fermion anomalies are described by an anomaly polynomial and phases built from reduced Dirac eta invariants. The construction extends from physical Laurent series with poles of order at most two to arbitrary Laurent poles, enabling the spectrum-level argument.

Estimate flux scaling from cubic intersections and generic flux contractions, then combine it with empirical lower estimates for the distance of a stretched mirror Kähler cone from the origin. The final charge estimate substitutes this distance for ||Im z||.

A Bloch–Messiah decomposition writes the real symmetric symplectic matrix M using positive reciprocal eigenvalue pairs and an orthogonal symplectic rotation U. Boundary behavior is investigated by sending an eigenvalue to infinity and tracking rotated flux components.
Use W=∫Ω∧G₃ with G₃=F₃−τH₃. The no-scale F-term minimum is equivalent to *G₃=iG₃, expressed as a flux-vector matrix equation; there N_flux=s H₃ᵀMH₃, with M the positive-definite Hodge-star matrix.

Evolves the photon polarization density matrix, expressed through I,Q,U,V, using a quantum Boltzmann equation. It separates a forward-scattering commutator linear in the interaction Hamiltonian from a collision double commutator quadratic in it.

The appendix evaluates the one-loop amplitude using dimensional regularization, Feynman parameters, gamma-matrix identities and transverse photon-polarization properties, then inserts the resulting effective Hamiltonian into the density-matrix evolution.

Constructs line-of-sight E/B transfer functions weighted by visibility, polarization source and spherical Bessel functions, with cos κ and sin κ respectively. Cross spectra integrate products of transfer functions against the scalar primordial power spectrum.

The global argument uses auxiliary Wick rotation, exceptional sets of small resolutions, adjunction for their local neighborhoods, and an explicitly conjectural analogy with the Tian–Yau complement construction.
Localization is analyzed through a Schrödinger-like graviton equation and a δ(z) well induced by the metric's |z| dependence. Distributional Ricci terms require matching localized matter sources.

The reviewed axilaton construction solves an Einstein–Friedan equation sourced by angular axion–dilaton variation. The equation is interpreted as the lowest-order condition for vanishing worldsheet metric beta function; warp factors are supplied as expansions.

Implements symmetric-phase Feynman rules in FeynArts, generates relevant two-, three- and four-point diagrams in Fermi ξ-gauges, and evaluates them with an in-house Mathematica program. The authors report gauge-parameter independence and UV/IR finiteness at leading nonvanishing order.

Uses EFT threshold reasoning to assess θ̄ versus higher-dimensional CP violation. EDM phenomenology imports nonperturbative nucleon estimates and chiral-EFT pion/nuclear relations, including dn=−(1.5±0.7)×10⁻³ θ̄ e fm and the adopted range dp=−(1±0.5)dn.

Expands arg det of the effective quark matrices through two loops, retaining both irreducible two-loop terms and reducible products of one-loop corrections. Separate unitary rotations put nonhermitian isosinglet masses into a real diagonal basis.

The withdrawn argument first rescales all Ramond potentials and F₀ by μ, holding other fields fixed. It writes Vμ=−μ²(LR+LCS)−μLWZ−L′NS−LDBI and applies first- and second-derivative minimum conditions at μ=1.

Dimensional reduction separates the Einstein–Hilbert term from the remaining Neveu–Schwarz action using R₁₀=e⁻²ᴬR+R₆+warp-derivative terms and the volume factor e⁴ᴬ. The potential is identified as minus the remaining reduced Lagrangian contributions.

A second proposed variation shifts A and φ by lnλ and rescales the Ramond-potential components with three or four external indices by λ⁴. The resulting quartic polynomial in λ is analyzed separately for LWZ=0 and LWZ>0.

The effective theory matches magnetic masses to moduli-dependent FI terms and gauge couplings. Brane separation is represented by a trilinear superpotential, with physical Yukawa couplings and matter Kähler metrics determining F-term masses and quartic terms.

The authors minimize the D-term over area ratios, analyze canonically normalized moduli masses, and numerically minimize the waterfall-corrected potential. Lambert-W branches describe the original volume-potential extrema.

Annulus and Möbius amplitudes, expressed through theta functions and SO(2) characters, determine the charged open-string spectrum. Magnetic oscillator shifts encode Landau levels and internal spin couplings; Wilson lines and separations supply positive mass contributions.

The QFT evidence includes a reported 1+1-dimensional modular/Cardy argument: a temporal symmetry insertion becomes a spatially twisted sector, giving Z(β,g)/Z(β)≈exp[-2πLΔg/β]. A separate heuristic studies large tensor powers of a faithful representation using character asymptotics.

Evaluate the twisted thermal trace using topological Wilson lines and asymptotic symmetry operators. Conjugation invariance and Schur's lemma give a Wilson-line expectation proportional to the identity; deforming its endpoint around the contractible thermal circle and using representation separation gives Z(β,g)=Z(β)δ(g) within the saddle argument.

Expand the twisted trace in irreducible characters, apply finite-group Schur orthogonality, and take an inverse Laplace transform to extract representation-resolved densities. The identity Σα dα²=|G| supplies the normalization check.

Obtain p(q) by Fourier transforming ⟨exp(iαQR)⟩; no replicas are required for this probability distribution. Bosonization expresses the charge insertion through endpoint vertex operators, whose correlators give approximately Gaussian probabilities for large intervals.

Use concavity and Araki–Lieb inequalities to bound the entropy of the holonomy-averaged state. In the strong-coupling examples, integrate out gauge fields to impose vanishing currents inside gravity, then evaluate bath vertex correlators with induced Dirichlet conditions and the method of images.

For WZW matter, diagonalize group elements into the Cartan subalgebra, use the free-field current representation, and integrate characters against the Haar/Vandermonde measure. The resulting weak-coupling matrix integral yields a Casimir-weighted representation distribution.

Linear scalar perturbations of excited Nariai reduce to a Legendre equation for symmetric-branch endpoints. Separate near-vacuum Bessel analyses test whether nontrivial bounces can terminate exactly at a potential minimum.

Integrate inward from approximately 10⁻⁵ away from each horizon toward positive f, match at the maximum of f, and use a Newton algorithm to adjust horizon data. The paper reports satisfactory smoothness after optimizing parameters to about three significant digits.

Vary a symmetry-reduced action and impose the remaining constraint. Schwarzschild gauge R = r applies only where R′ ≠ 0; the general gauge δ = 0 retains R(r). Regular horizon Taylor expansions supply integration data.

Test ordinary convexity through nonnegative second derivatives on twice-differentiable intervals, then infer superadditivity using the imported Petrovic theorem with Δ(0)=0. At kinks, the source requires returning to the definition rather than applying the derivative criterion across the singular point.

Combine analytic leading semiclassical expressions, numerical next-order sums and plots, one-loop superadditivity differences, and small-/large-charge limits. The authors use semiclassics particularly to bridge the intermediate regime where ordinary perturbation and large-charge EFT are insufficient.

Use fixed-charge semiclassical expansions Δ(Q)=λ*^{-1}Δ−1(λ*Q)+Δ0(λ*Q)+… at small fixed-point coupling and fixed coupling-times-charge. These resum leading charge powers at every ordinary perturbative order. Cylinder calculations use a Weyl map; the large-N O(N) test instead uses direct operator-insertion results.

Combines an imported IIB2 stabilization bound involving K^(3), saxions and dual saxions with estimates obtained from Kreuzer–Skarke statistics through mirror symmetry. This is a conditional scaling argument using prior results, rather than a new enumeration of flux vacua.

Uses a stretched mirror Kähler cone to relate distance from moduli-space boundaries to the minimum saxion norm. A log-log-linear statistical fit supplies d_min proportional to c times a power β of h2,1.

For spherical complex-field stars, use Φ(r,t) = φ(r)e^{−iωt} with a static metric, reduce Einstein–Klein–Gordon to radial equations, and shoot outward to satisfy localization conditions. Frequency eigenstates are labeled so the n-th state has n − 1 radial nodes.

Stability methods include charge-conserving perturbations of scalar and metric, radial mode-frequency analysis, turning points dM/dφ_c = dN/dφ_c = 0, and full nonlinear Einstein–Klein–Gordon evolution.

In nonrelativistic condensate descriptions, Schrödinger–Poisson and the Madelung transformation yield continuity and Euler equations with quantum pressure. Linearizing the fluid equations gives the Jeans dispersion relation.

Applies black-hole entropy fluctuations, including the imported modular-Hamiltonian variance relation, to cosmological perturbations. Estimates subsequent density growth, evaporation, reheating and the PBH abundance required at matter–radiation equality, without calculating a merger distribution.

Models horizon equilibrium through a conjectured cutoff 1+1-dimensional CFT and fast scrambling. Relativity is implemented by requiring matching entanglement spectra for density matrices assigned to overlapping causal diamonds.

Uses Schwarzschild–de Sitter horizon entropy to obtain an entropy deficit relative to empty de Sitter space. For a small black hole, the statistical weight is approximately exp(−2πMR), identifying localized objects as constrained states and yielding the de Sitter temperature.

Adapts the Aasen–Mong–Fendley construction by imposing local defect commutation relations on complementary sets of tetrahedra. Variables belonging to links created or removed by a deformation are summed, while externally coupled variables remain arbitrary. Mathematica was used to find the weights.

Uses explicit junction-weight identities and topology-changing crossing relations, including complementary solid tori and disconnected three-disks, to evaluate closed defect configurations and connected sums.

Uses formal E7(7) covariance to trade nonzero axions for a changed embedding tensor. Representation branching and SO(1,1) grading show that the transformation generates only a linear deformation δΘ in (35,1) with charge +3, itself satisfying the quadratic constraints.

The appendix proves restricted-sector potential invariance by expanding into the original potential, deformation potential and bilinear cross term. Antisymmetry of the relevant scalar-dressed so(6) matrix makes the latter two contributions vanish under the stated commutation condition.

Computes complete scalar, vector and gravitino mass spectra of the four-dimensional maximal theory for the deformed N = 4 vacuum, using them to classify residual symmetry, supersymmetry and BF stability.

Extract anomalous dimensions from Lorentz-invariant phase-space integrals of products of tree amplitudes across two-particle cuts. Project onto the rational bubble contribution and add collinear terms to account for scaleless bubbles with cancelling UV and IR parts.

Implement the rational-part projection through a spinor parameterization of two-body phase space, contour residues and Hermite polynomial reduction, extracting rational primitives without computing logarithmic terms.

Use little-group scaling, factorization and modified-helicity addition to constrain amplitudes. Supersymmetric Ward identities supply vanishing-amplitude proofs; angular-momentum decompositions further restrict cuts and stress-tensor renormalization.

Minimize the KKLT/LVS scalar potentials to obtain bulk curvature scales and insert the NS5 tension, calculated as brane tension times wrapped S³ volume. The LVS modulus is determined numerically, using the exact stationary relation rather than its leading approximation.

Compute the induced metric and extrinsic curvature on each side, then solve the Israel junction conditions for the wall tension and Friedmann equation. Extract Λ3 from the radius-independent part of H3².

For H fluxes, Z=(p+1)A+βpφ reduces the constraint to (Z')²=Δ²e^(2Z)+E, an auxiliary Newtonian energy equation. Setting f=e^(−Z) produces elementary branches. Analytic continuation to cosmology reverses the exponential potential and produces a cosh solution.

Solves first-order Killing-spinor equations to identify supersymmetric subsets. A separate DBI/Wess–Zumino probe-brane analysis examines the force near the singular origin, including a nonrelativistic approximation.

Derives a reduced one-dimensional action and field equations, choosing harmonic gauge B=(p+1)A+(D−p−2)C and retaining the B equation as a Hamiltonian constraint. The h-flux contribution is inserted through the higher-dimensional equations rather than the simple symmetric reduced action.

Exponentiated jumps define Čech transition functions. Double-sine difference equations identify Riemann–Hilbert jump potentials; changes of local trivialization produce Rogers-dilogarithm transitions, followed by a conformal-limit comparison.

Laplace integration, Fourier-transform unitarity, contour deformation and residue summation relate the Borel sum to a Woronowicz integral and triple-sine function. Hankel contours around strings of poles determine Stokes jumps.

The authors construct the Borel transform through a Hadamard product and its contour-integral representation, using Bernoulli and polylogarithm identities to establish convergence and meromorphic continuation.
For heterotic orbifolds, use modular-integral threshold corrections and estimate their moduli-dependent N=2-subsector contribution from the subsector spectrum, choosing order-one torus moduli.

For the mirror quintic, obtain the gauge kinetic matrix from holomorphic three-form periods, perform an area average over complex-structure moduli, and use symplectic transformations to select a genus-two Siegel fundamental-domain representative.

Generate random superextremal mass spectra on charge lattices, determine which states lie below the species cutoff, and sum their one-loop thresholds. An analytic ratio distribution for paired masses and a continuum half-ellipse approximation estimate the variance.

Add flux-induced D terms, minimize transverse volume directions, and reduce to an effective volume potential. A different implicit parametrization treats moderate moduli; the appendix supplies an unexpanded potential and illustrative numerical plots.

Compute the supergravity F-term potential from corrected K and W; expand in inverse volume and perturbative parameters, separating perturbative, non-perturbative and mixed contributions. Solve approximate F-flatness equations using Lambert-W branches; large τ2 selects W_{−1}.

Construct (0,1) heterotic and (1,1) type II linear sigma models, integrate out massive fields, and analyze large-P effective superpotentials. Compare supersymmetric indices, reflection-twisted Lefschetz numbers, and D-brane K-theory invariants.

Reduce near the Hagedorn radius to a light winding field χ coupled to the circle-radius field ϕ. Integrating out ϕ gives a nonlocal attractive interaction and an eigenvalue problem; numerical shooting constructs profiles, while amplitude/size rescalings test existence and instability.

Use the dilaton equation to reduce the tree-level on-shell action to a boundary term. Generate charged backgrounds through shifts, quotients and T-dualities, represented asymptotically by O(2,2), and differentiate the transformed action for thermodynamics.

Follow families of minima under mass/cosmological-constant scans. For quintessence, evaluate the field-metric gradient norm of the two-scalar potential and test the absolute-value bound, especially near ∂R V = 0.

Construct the three-dimensional radion potential from the cosmological tree term and the one-loop Casimir energy, using a KK sum involving K₂. Numerically track extrema and their vacuum energies as neutrino masses vary.

Constructs explicit toric hypersurface/complete-intersection and Tate models; computes coefficient cohomologies, including rational representatives regular on the hypersurface. Uses Chern-class intersections for Euler numbers and Kulikov-type semistable degenerations with birational transformations for heterotic limits.

Uses the imported Hartshorne–Serre extension presentation 0→O→V₂→O(D)⊗I_z→0 after a line-bundle twist. Section existence and character are studied through pushforwards, global bundle sections and quotient line bundles.

Use N(ϕ)=∫[ϕ0,ϕ]H/(8.8Γ^(1/4)f)dϕ to locate CMB horizon crossing. Scan potential parameters, fixing the power-spectrum amplitude and imposing the reported spectral-index window and theoretical consistency conditions.

Locate minima and maxima, then locally fit a tilted cosine V=μ³ϕ+Λ⁴cos(ϕ/f+θ)+C. Infer μ, Λ and f from extrema and calculate Γ=A exp(−SE), using the authors' previously published approximation rather than a generic thin-wall approximation.

Import simulation-based relations ΔR²≈0.06(Γ/H⁴)^(−5/12) and ϕ̇=−8.8Γ^(1/4)f. Obtain the scalar tilt from the variation of Γ and H; interpolate the discrete rates to evaluate derivatives and integrals.

Extend eigenvalue inequalities through Rayleigh min-max principles, Lipschitz approximation, coarea inequalities and heat-semigroup arguments; analyze surface examples using magnetic Schrödinger and Legendre equations.

Translate the universal spin-two mass operator into a Bakry–Émery weighted Laplacian; use synthetic curvature bounds, optimal transport and infinitesimal Hilbertianity to accommodate specified singular spaces.
Choose finitely many function levels, build disjoint band functions, invoke min–max, and apply coarea to a monotone transform. The paper adapts this sequence to the RCD calculus.
Combine a punctured curvature bound with optimal-transport avoidance and quadraticity of the energy. In this paper the operation is adapted to exact D6 cones and a logarithmic D7 end.

Localize the Rayleigh quotient, threshold squared test functions, and approximate a finite spectral subspace by compactly supported functions. The supplied infinite-volume argument additionally invokes a compressed heat family whose semigroup property needs justification.
Separate the five-brane source data into two distant groups along the strip. The brane-free interval is the prospective bridge, but the quantitative large-ξ analysis is outside the supplied window.

For the Family III uplift, the authors guess a ten-dimensional metric, compare its graviton spectrum with the KK result, and impose type IIB field equations on ansätze for the remaining fields. They report satisfaction of the equations and Bianchi identities.

Analytic results cover all levels on Family III, the generic ell=0 tower, and selected low-level graviton towers. The numerical database covers ell=0,…,3 and n=0,±1,±2,±3; its general grid uses 0.05≤e^(2phi)≤2 and 0≤chi≤1 in steps of 0.05, with T=2pi.

Group-theory branching determines multiplet content: tensor the lowest-level fields with harmonic representations [0,ell,0]_(2n), remove Goldstones and Goldstinos, and branch to the residual symmetry. ExFT-derived mass matrices supply eigenvalues, subsequently translated to conformal dimensions and assembled into supermultiplets.

The positive-energy wavefunction grows on the real z axis. The construction continues z into normalizable complex Stokes wedges, sets y=−iz and q=i pz, and applies a further non-unitary similarity transformation generated by a Hermitian Q to obtain an ordinary positive oscillator.

Spatial modes are reduced to the Pais–Uhlenbeck oscillator with omega_i=sqrt(spatial momentum squared+Mi^2), z replacing phi, and x=zdot. Ostrogradski or Dirac-constraint methods give its canonical two-oscillator Hamiltonian.

A fermion functional integral is used to motivate an induced term proportional to R_mu_nu R^mu_nu−R^2/3, with a logarithmically divergent coefficient. This is presented as a route from locally conformal matter to a fourth-order gravitational action.

Generalized dimensional analysis compares Higgs-dependent and Higgs-independent scalar potentials, or their derivatives, and supplements this balance with Higgs-loop naturalness and experimental coupling bounds.

Cosmological estimates use misalignment production, the classical equation φ̈+3Hφ̇+∂V/∂φ=0, radiation-dominated evolution, and separate local/global potential regions. The QCD implementation matches the gluonic interaction to a chiral potential.

The paper uses the imported extremality/on-shell-action relation and reports explicit comparisons with perturbed metrics for quartic curvature and dilatonic examples. Massive-scalar tree-level matching illustrates cancellations among individually sign-indefinite operators.

One-loop beta functions are extracted from four-photon unitarity cuts and scalar bubble coefficients. Helicity selection eliminates logarithmic running of the Riemann–FF operator at this order; absent φF² couplings, the logarithmic F⁴ structure is the square of the photon stress tensor.

Analytic forward dispersion relations and the generalized optical theorem express Wilson-coefficient tensors through sums of quadratic products of real UV-amplitude matrices. Tensor symmetrization then exposes sums of squares on appropriately factorized backgrounds.

Explicit differentiation and inversion of the corrected Kähler metric, contraction identities, and a degree-one homogeneity argument produce compact reformulations of the supergravity F-term potential.

Stationarity and odd-axion Hessians are analyzed in real coordinates, including {tα,bᵃ,ρ̃α,ĉᵃ}. Minimization uses independent tα inside the Kähler cone, where the paper states that the map to four-cycle coordinates is bijective.

Construct the EFT basis using local spinor-helicity amplitudes; perturb Maxwell and Einstein equations and locate corrected horizons. Compute Wald entropy and renormalized Euclidean free energies, including leading canonical corrections evaluated on uncorrected solutions.

Build nonlinear KK reduction ansätze using Sasaki–Einstein geometry, gauge the U(1)R isometry, and evaluate ten-dimensional Hodge duals and field equations. Explore dynamical γ through an expansion with even powers in metric/dilaton/five-form and odd powers in three-forms.

Compute six-dimensional Seeley–DeWitt b6 coefficients and sum a functional Schrödinger anomaly prescription over complete supermultiplets. Construct differential operators acting on the large-N single-trace index in its high-temperature limit.

Solve flavor–gauge, flavor–flavor and flavor–gravitational anomaly cancellation using generalized Green–Schwarz terms from existing tensors, including the prospective flavor-vector contributions. The search forbids new hypers charged solely under the added flavor algebra.

A shortcut adds an arbitrary u(1), solves charge/anomaly constraints while permitting formally negative u(1)-only singlet multiplicities, and uses these deficits to identify candidate nonabelian flavor embeddings. Separately, center gauging is obstructed if some tensor charge b gives Σ_i(b·b_i)α_i k_i²∉Z.

Polarized detector-pair timestreams form Q/U maps. Matrix purification suppresses E-to-B leakage; inverse-noise apodization, Fourier transformation and rotation to E/B yield angular spectra. Different sky masks are incorporated in bandpower window functions.

Jackknife split-map null tests and spectral-stability comparisons assess consistency. Failed preliminary null tests led to exclusion of November 2016 Keck data and BICEP3 focal-plane tile 1; these removals preceded inspection of non-jackknife spectra.

An approximate Hamimeche–Lewis joint likelihood is explored with COSMOMC MCMC for r plus seven foreground parameters. Covariances use 499 signal/noise simulations, explicitly zeroing specified signal–noise and inter-experiment noise covariance terms.

Reviewed semiclassical backreaction calculations determine quantum fields and classical geometry self-consistently through the semiclassical Einstein equation. The methodological history includes closed-time-path/in-in Schwinger–Keldysh techniques; including stress-tensor fluctuations leads to stochastic sources in the Einstein–Langevin equation.

The reviewed open-system treatment of an interacting λΦ⁴ field in a closed Robertson–Walker universe uses a coarse-grained effective action to compute how inhomogeneous modes affect the scale factor and homogeneous field mode. In that example, minisuperspace is valid only when this backreaction is small.

For Berger’s Gowdy example, gravitational-wave amplitudes are canonically quantized, an adiabatic vacuum is chosen, and adiabatic regularization supplies finite stress-tensor expectation values as sources for the classical background.

Use Clausen identities and their twisted generalizations to relate third-order K3 equations to second-order elliptic equations. First-order ε-expansions, together with a period constraint, replace the required second parameter derivatives.
Start from the Frobenius fundamental period with auxiliary parameters ρ_i, obtain other periods by parameter differentiation, and resum one modulus into generalized hypergeometric functions.

Beyond ordinary hypergeometry, use integer Apéry-like recurrences and their generating functions, algebraic changes of argument, and hypergeometric transformations to reduce the needed derivatives to the same elliptic toolkit.

Use the GVW-derived superpotential with thraxions imposing homology constraints, express conifold moduli in terms of thraxions, and insert the effective superpotential into the N=1 F-term potential with perturbative and nonperturbative stabilization corrections.
Analyze SU(3) intrinsic torsion classes and supersymmetry relations between fluxes, internal spinors and torsion to diagnose departures from conformal CY geometry.
Scan favorable CICY orientifold conifold transitions, filtering for unchanged O-plane configurations, absence of frozen conifolds, and optionally simultaneous O3/O7 presence.

Use misalignment abundance estimates and scans over microscopic parameters to obtain mass–abundance bands. Representative LVS ranges include W0=1–100, nonperturbative prefactors 10^-4–10^4 and brane ranks 1–10; observational exclusions are imported from the literature available to the paper.

Compute axion kinetic metrics from the Kähler potential, canonically normalise fields, and diagonalise the mass matrix where mixing matters. Potentials arise from ED3, ED1 and ED3/ED1 effects, gaugino condensation, or warped flux backreaction.

Reduce the curve equations using the ϕ isometry and a constant-radius ansatz, then test internal and radial stationarity against the full action. The source's proposed reduction is not verified by its printed coefficients.

Expand the full fluxed D7 action, retaining angular dependence of both the embedding and gauge connection. Project onto harmonic multiplets and diagonalize the resulting blocks; singlet-only calculations would miss the unstable modes.

Solve the D7 gauge equation, vary the embedding while holding intrinsic flux fixed, and only then substitute the flux solution. Expand about a constant-position solution at fixed integrated S2 flux to extract singlet masses.

Integrate the probe equations from initial data, exploit reflection conditions where available, and switch the dependent variable near turning points. The procedure follows bent 5-branes through regions inaccessible to a single graph parametrization.

Expand the non-Abelian D5 action near a displaced pole at fixed x, keeping leading mass, cubic dielectric and quartic commutator terms. Representation decomposition then reduces the fluctuation Hessian to finite SU(2) blocks.

Take the regular boundary limit of the unfluxed five-brane action, uniformize its DBI square root and integrate a first-order embedding proposal. Check the full equation and admissible endpoints for the particular web; do not apply this formula to fluxed probes or X≠1.

Rather than determine every KK mass, exhibit a normalizable nonzero mode at the AdS scale, which bounds the first massive KK level from above. The source implements this using decoupled spin-2 fluctuations, with details deferred to its unsupplied Section 7.

Expand at fixed source charges near one pole, cancel leading tension and charge terms, canonically normalize the surviving radial fluctuation and evaluate directional limits. The operation is local and therefore does not require the global form of Σ.

Evaluate the charged wall's potential on a Poincaré slice and differentiate it in radial and internal directions. Boundary-directed force diagnoses brane expulsion. For internally extended walls, solve a curve embedding rather than replacing the wall by an internal point.

Separate angular harmonics, rescale the internal coefficient, use a background differential identity, and match effective eigenvalues. Physical squared masses then transfer between siblings at fixed harmonic label and fixed underlying internal data.

Fix the internal coordinate at a stationary point, then compare electric expansion against tension and curvature using Euclidean-energy conservation or a spherical action variation. The two constructions are related only under the stated absence of internal motion.

Pull back background fields, retain the specified worldvolume flux, expand around an embedding, normalize the kinetic operator and diagonalize fluctuations. The dilaton conversion Φ=2φ in Sections 3–4 is necessary when comparing with Section 5.3.

Survey curve embeddings numerically, continue them across coordinate turning points and branch cuts, and test whether a complete S5-wrapped configuration avoids the AdS boundary and has finite action.

Expand the radial ansatz to first order in α′, solve coupled linear ODEs, and fix integration constants by horizon regularity and asymptotic Minkowski conditions. Obtain heterotic fields through the proposed first-order S-duality map and field/coordinate redefinitions.

Compute temperature, charges, potentials, Iyer-Wald entropy and Euclidean action, with a separate treatment of Lorentz Chern-Simons contributions in the heterotic entropy. The paper reports a first-law check through O(α′).

Extract the probe static potential and its large-radius falloff, separate graviton, dilaton and two-form contributions in Einstein frame, and reexpress the force coefficient in physical fixed-charge variables before expanding near extremality.

Construct C_sl(2)=exp(x·N−) e(y)^−1 C∞ e(y) exp(−x·N−), with e(y)=exp[½Σ log(y^k)N_k^0]. Flux-axion polynomials and weight decompositions simplify self-duality equations; their solutions seed numerical refinement with the nilpotent-orbit Hodge star.
Test consequential identities against full starting expressions and simple limits. Preserve both the printed expression and the failed result, rather than silently substituting a familiar formula.

Project original nilpotent generators using the compatible hierarchy gradings, rather than completing each monodromy independently. This removes components that obstruct commutation with the other triples and supplies the operators needed for Hodge-star scaling.
Use mirror topological data to construct leading periods and their monodromies. Rational symplectic removal of real lower-degree terms simplifies the algebra but requires care with the flux lattice.

Construct leading vector subspaces rather than retaining only leading coefficients of Ω. Overall exponential factors in spanning sections can be divided out, preserving essential Hodge directions in an algebraic limiting description.

Compute the generating coefficients, build P_k recursively, expand both sides of the master identity, and match each bidegree without commuting operators. The fourfold application produces (B.4)–(B.5), subject to structural conditions whose full definitions are outside this window.

Solve a simpler boundary constraint first and then restore specified classes of corrections. In this paper the constraint is flux self-duality and the leading simplification is fixed by compatible sl(2) representations.
Construct boundary Hodge subspaces from a compatible split filtration, assign their exact Hodge eigenvalues, and restore leading saxion and axion dependence by explicit conjugations.

Decompose the cohomology representation into irreducible sl(2) blocks and weight eigenspaces. The physical boundary construction must additionally select a completion compatible with the limiting Hodge structure.

An imported iterative linear-algebra algorithm starts from limiting Hodge filtrations and commuting log-monodromies, constructs monodromy weight filtrations and Deligne splittings, rotates to sl(2)-splittings, and extracts mutually commuting sl(2) triples and the boundary Hodge decomposition.

Compute δ from the grading's conjugation defect, rotate and recompute the splitting, then calculate ζ in that new splitting. Direct reuse of the original δ components in the ζ formulas violates the prescribed algorithm.

Begin with all boundary coordinates, split their mixed Hodge structure, set the last coordinate to a reference value through a nilpotent exponential, and repeat. Each stage yields a cumulative grading needed for commuting triples.

Compute the period matrix, assemble its Hodge-star blocks, and impose flux self-duality in a consistent symplectic convention. The supplied formulas contain transpose and lower-period-sign ambiguities that prevent unconditional identification across sections.

Kinematic-basis projection of the equations of motion and covariant potential Hessian relates tangent/mixed Hessian elements to turning and slow-roll parameters. The normal Hessian projection remains model dependent.

A differential-evolution survey uses rapid-turn, positive-heavy-mass and empirical cost functions. Classical trajectories are evolved with Inflation.jl at several hundred minimizing points for each cost-function choice; the survey includes literature models and ad hoc constructions.

Expand the N=1 supergravity effective action about its AdS minimum, canonically normalise fields and diagonalise masses. For degenerate double traces, extract an effective anomalous-dimension matrix from mixed correlators and use its eigenvalues rather than individual matrix entries.

Use Mellin representations of four-point functions to extract n=0 large-spin anomalous dimensions. Leading contributions come from t-channel exchanges and cubic couplings; three-point coefficients are obtained through Witten diagrams in embedding formalism.

Uses an imported RG-improved one-loop expression for vacuum-energy running from the KK cutoff to the deep infrared, containing quadratic supertrace contributions and logarithmic terms involving fourth powers of masses.

Combines a supergravity supertrace identity, including background vacuum energy and Kähler/gauge-kinetic curvature terms, with the LVS vacuum-energy estimate. Keeping dominant terms gives a spectral uplift criterion and an upper bound on compactification volume.

Evaluate a Gaussian field-state functional on a trial bubble profile to estimate overlap suppression. The stated bubble exponent is recoverable only after explicitly assuming the appropriate free-vacuum kernel; the supplied expression itself fails this check.

Reduce a trial bubble family to one coordinate, estimate its inertia and barrier, and integrate the under-barrier momentum. This supplies a conditional scaling argument for a frozen model, without solving the rolling field-theory transition.

Transform the initial packet to momentum space, apply the known free phases, and transform back. The operation yields drift and spreading exactly for a free particle. Applying it to a rolling packet requires a justified treatment of the nonzero potential.

Choose a one-scale trial bubble, estimate its gradient and volume energies, and balance them. The method produces a parametric radius; it does not determine a bounce profile, a rate prefactor, or a thin-wall surface tension.

Uses two distinct Legendre transformations: with x=|φc|² and y=m², Υ(x)=V(√x) and varpi(y)=ω(√y) are conjugate; transforming ω with respect to m gives fixed-charge free-energy density. Supremum conjugation is distinguished from stationary, potentially complex continuation.

Computes spectral zeta functions through Mellin transforms and heat-kernel expansions. Sphere calculations combine convergent small-m series, asymptotic large-m series, recursion between even-dimensional spheres and Borel/resurgence constructions with principal-value prescriptions.

Reviews the positive-measure Hölder argument for convexity of the connected generating functional, effective action and effective potential. Convexity of the latter is then used as a necessary consistency condition for unitarity.

Derives a one-dimensional effective action and supplements its equations with the rr Einstein equation, interpreted as zero radial Hamiltonian. The authors report equivalence with the ten-dimensional equations evaluated on their ansatz.

Uses Fefferman–Graham boundary analysis and scalar mass diagonalization. The retained masses are M²L²=6,6,20,20; normalizable exponents obey Δ(Δ−3)=M²L², giving two pairwise-degenerate eigenspaces and four free boundary coefficients.

Numerically integrates inward from the AdS boundary and matches AdS, intermediate dilaton-bubble and smeared-D2 regimes. The imposed relations 3c₁−4c₂=0 and c₃+12c₄=0 select the intermediate regime with constant 3U−φ/4.
For flat slices, separates F=e^(3A)f(ϕ,χ). The HJ equation becomes V=−3f²+2Kⁱʲ∂ᵢf∂ⱼf, interpreted as fake supergravity. The actual supersymmetric solution is fSUSY=e^(K/2)|W|.

Builds local Taylor expansions of f around critical points, chooses Hessian branches, and computes through order 15. First-order HJ equations are then integrated numerically to obtain flat domain-wall profiles.

Reduces radial scalar-gravity dynamics to a one-dimensional Hamiltonian system. Canonical momenta are gradients of an HJ generating function F, which satisfies the zero-Hamiltonian constraint; the authors report agreement with the original four-dimensional equations for their ansatz.

Find fixed points numerically: simple subsystems use Mathematica NSolve, with completeness checks reported by the authors. More complicated systems first solve the matter equations at approximate gravitational fixed-point coordinates, then use those roots to initialize FindRoot for the coupled system.

Use linear background-field splits, harmonic gauge, and a Type I regulator with Litim profile Rk(z)=(k²−z)θ(k²−z). Interaction vertices are generated using xAct; the retained projection receives contributions from 18 traces.

Project the formally exact Wetterich equation onto the retained invariants. Expand the inverse regulated Hessian in background structures and evaluate the resulting traces with off-diagonal heat-kernel techniques.

Convert candidate internal spectra to masses and AdS energies, then simplify absolute values only after imposing the source's representation-Casimir threshold. The restriction is algebraic and leaves low-Casimir modes outside this partial analysis.

Differentiate an orthonormal frame, express its anholonomy in frame components, and solve the linear torsion-free equation for omega. The sign discrepancy in (5.18b) must be tracked separately when reproducing the calculation.

Project, contract, and square an assumed eigenmode equation while retaining all zero-component cases. Solve the necessary polynomial, then distinguish candidate roots from modes whose representations and existence have actually been established.

Expand the shifted rough Laplacian, substitute the coset curvature, and cancel the isotropy Casimir. Project the surviving invariant endomorphisms into irreducible sectors of a group preserving the structure constants and metric.

Use homogeneous-space harmonic analysis and group-theoretical equations rather than explicitly solving differential equations. Requiring the left-squashed fields to form N = 1 AdS4 supermultiplets eliminates some false roots produced by the spectral method.

Contract the three-form with a and c, subtract the scalar trace from its symmetric contraction, and project transversality into 7 and 14 equations. Components remain coupled until the spectral equations are applied.

Normalize octonionic intertwiners by idempotency, resolve curvature with G2 projectors, and use the torsionful derivative algebra. This supplies component equations without constructing explicit harmonic wavefunctions.

Contract with the invariant spinor and gamma matrices to replace a constrained vector-spinor equation by a rank-two tensor equation. Translate transversality before taking divergences, so the resulting vector satisfies the conditions of the curl identity.

Introduce the universal Laplacian Δ = −□ − R_abcd Σ^ab Σ^cd on Spin(7) representations. It equals the Hodge Laplacian on forms and the Lichnerowicz operator on symmetric rank-2 tensors; on transverse 3-forms, Q = *d satisfies Q² = Δ3. These identities organize the internal spectral problem.

In 9d, use the piecewise cubic 5d prepotential: its second derivative determines the inverse gauge coupling and its third derivative the Chern-Simons coefficient. Single-valuedness around the interval's double cover requires the total level jump ∑i ci=0.

Wrap spatial probe directions on a torus to obtain quantum mechanics on the moduli space. Relate energies to Laplacian eigenvalues and argue that a continuous spectrum produces unacceptable entropy relative to a black-hole bound.

Combine ADHM and exceptional-instanton input with worldvolume SCFT data and mass deformations. In 8d, use Rank≤4(2a−c); for the interacting SU(2) small-instanton theory, a=11/24 and c=1/2 give Rank≤5/3, excluding integer ranks greater than one.
The paper generates the data by elliptic-curve multiplication of explicitly supplied seed sections and evaluation of normalized component orders at fixed loci.

Generate section multiples in a fixed seed, normalize their components, track pseudo-charge and center labels, and compare local valuations. Independent ways of producing the same charge-center pair provide consistency tests.

Add sections fiberwise, evaluate explicit doubling or addition expressions, then clear denominators and remove common weighted factors before calculating local valuations. This constructs multiples on the same Weierstrass fibration.

Hold the fibration and matter locus fixed, vary the integer section multiplier, normalize the resulting coordinates, and compare their valuations with predictions at effective charge mq. This tests scaling without constructing a new high-charge compactification.

Construct analogous elliptic curves by replacing matter-locus parameters with prime integers, then compare section vanishing with p-adic elliptic divisibility sequence valuations. For nonabelian cases, subtract codimension-one contributions to account for removable common coordinate factors.

Compute Weierstrass valuations and split conditions, identify generic and enhanced ADE types, and branch the enhanced adjoint. When this shortcut is unreliable, resolve the fiber and determine weights from curve–divisor intersections.

Evaluate recursively generated division polynomials on an integral point, then study their valuations. Comparing these values with normalized section coordinates requires checking equation conventions and removing allowable common factors.

Classify the fiber types, infer center labels from section valuations, and solve for |q|. Conversely, fix the representation and global sector, determine μ, and predict section orders. Use global charge cosets as a separate sign constraint.

Compute multiples mŝ of seed generating sections and extract vanishing orders at known matter loci. These non-generating sections supply pseudo-charges; obtaining the same pseudo-charge and center label through independent routes provides consistency evidence.

Given the transformed EDS valuation, multiply it by the inverse ramification degree and add the reported discriminant-dependent term. The paper imports this operation from a cited theorem and applies it to one curve transformation; the complete theorem is not reproduced here.

Model codimension-two and codimension-one behavior with separate arithmetic EDS sequences, then subtract their valuations to approximate normalized section orders. Retain arithmetic corrections unless their cancellation is established.

Apply the cited identity-reduction valuation formula, insert the x-coordinate valuation, and retain the entire S_m correction. The resulting expression remains indexed by m until the separate Appendix B replacement is imposed.

Combine absolute-charge information with section sums or sign-sensitive consistency constraints. The method returns only the signs fixed by those constraints and treats conjugate full-hypermultiplet descriptions appropriately.

Use the imported Euclidean on-shell-action prescription: evaluate four-derivative terms on the two-derivative solution to obtain leading free-energy corrections. Corrections to the solution contribute zero to the two-derivative on-shell action in this prescription.

Obtain scalar charges thermodynamically from μ^i = -4 G^{ij} ∂M/∂φ∞^j at fixed entropy and conserved charges. Subject to the stated zero-temperature condition, extremal mass derivatives suffice. For a preserved dilaton shift, Δμφ = -2aQ ∂QΔM + 2aP ∂PΔM at T=0 and φ∞=0.

For the generalized gauge kinetic function, promote its parameter ω to a transforming spurion to generate solutions at nonzero scalar VEV. The resulting complicated corrections are evaluated numerically point-by-point.

Use target-space covariant scalar equations and three SL(2,R) Noether currents to obtain first integrals, an algebraic semicircle relation and explicit radial profiles. Integrate sourced current equations over the interior to obtain surface matching conditions.

Expand the Einstein-frame metric and Weyl factor at large radius, transform to the relevant PPN coordinates and distinguish the gravitational mass inferred from Jordan-frame trajectories from the Einstein-frame integration constant.

Canonical field redefinitions turn kinetic singularities into stretched plateau potentials. For T-models, φ=√(6α)tanh(ϕ/√(6α)); expansion near the boundary identifies the plateau height and leading slope, whose nonzero exponential coefficient can be absorbed by shifting ϕ.

The paper overlays model trajectories on published observational confidence regions, commonly showing N_e=50 and 60. These comparisons illustrate how varying α, pole parameters, or nonminimal coupling changes n_s and r.

Use relative entropy S_Amax(R)(ω|ω∘E) as an operator-independent entropic order parameter. The reviewed certainty relation for a global pure state is S_R+S_R'=log λ, with each term between zero and log λ, where λ is the inclusion index.

Apply the double commutant theorem to complementary inclusions. Nonlocally generated operators are organized into sectors under left and right multiplication by additive operators, with fusion rules. Conditional expectations remove these sectors and generalize averaging over a symmetry group.
Construct Aadd(R) from algebras of balls covering R, and define Amax(R)=Aadd(R')'. Causality gives Aadd(R)⊆Amax(R); saturation for every region is the proposed completeness criterion.

Describe the D8/D6 system by non-closed worldvolume flux and a BIon transverse profile, using calibrations and DBI linearization. A separate four-dimensional decay argument compares scalar-field excursions and wall tensions with a supersymmetric transition, avoiding reliance solely on a thin-wall argument.

Construct localization corrections through Calabi–Yau Laplace equations for a three-form current and warp/dilaton profiles; adjust harmonic, co-exact and exact flux components to satisfy Bianchi identities and equations of motion at the retained order.

Evaluate membrane tension and effective flux coupling using dimensionally reduced DBI and Chern–Simons actions. Near the AdS boundary, Q = T identifies a marginal wall, while Q > T identifies a candidate expanding bubble.

Open-string power laws are inferred from η-function S-transformation asymptotics. Closed strings instead use the Kutasov–Seiberg identity and a Mellin/Eisenstein-series treatment of the full modular-invariant partition function; the discussion of nontrivial zeta-zero locations explicitly assumes the Riemann hypothesis.

The analysis splits mass levels into arithmetic progressions, expands Bessel functions, and evaluates geometric sums using Bernoulli/Euler polynomials. Singular contributions independent of subsector labels cancel through signed combinations and periodic P-function identities.

An imported Hardy–Ramanujan–Rademacher theorem computes coefficients of suitable finite Dedekind η-quotients using Bessel functions and periodic Kloosterman-like factors P_α. Its stated hypotheses include c_1>0, G(α)≥0, and n>n_0; exceptional low levels are treated separately.

One-loop heavy-particle thresholds are estimated using Gilkey–DeWitt heat-kernel coefficients. Local terms scale as m^4 in vacuum energy, m²R, and Planck-suppressed corrections to gravitino kinetic and mass terms. Coefficients are of order 1/(16π²), with possible mass logarithms, in dimensional regularization with minimal subtraction.

Metric and gravitino field redefinitions restore canonical kinetic terms before matching infrared parameters in K and W. Changes to the X kinetic normalization are absorbed into X rescalings; auxiliary fields are integrated rather than replaced throughout by fixed spurions.

The construction imports constrained-superfield descriptions: X²=0 removes the goldstino's scalar partner, XY=0 removes a matter fermion's scalar partner, and XW=0 removes the gaugino. A scalar chirality constraint removes its fermion and auxiliary component while retaining the scalar.
Cylinder Yang–Mills heat kernels, character expansions and holonomy integration express the partition function as a representation sum with Casimir-dependent weights.
Gaussian messenger integration, diagonalisation into φ±, numerical Fourier transformation, propagator pole analysis and Hubbard–Stratonovich source fields are used to analyse scalar correlators.
Schur, Hall–Littlewood and Kostka polynomials yield explicit partition sums; continuous Young diagrams and box densities provide large-rank saddle equations.

Expand D3 and M2/anti-M2 DBI plus Wess–Zumino probe actions at low velocity, in static gauge with transverse coordinates depending on time. Extract a potential and inspect its radial derivative for brane-jet repulsion.

Use eleven-dimensional uplift formulas for four-dimensional AdS critical points, determine the external three-form potential from the four-form flux, and evaluate the resulting M2 potential at each fixed point.
Solve the Janus background equations numerically and evaluate the D3 potential V = z^(−4)[f² + 4∫f^(5/2)dr]. The plotted diagnostic is z⁴∂rV.
The reduced matter Lagrangian is P(X,h) = KX + LX²/MPl⁴ − W, with X = −(∂h)²/2, K = Ĝ/(Ĝ² + 8αV̂), L = 2α/(Ĝ² + 8αV̂), and W = MPl⁴V̂/(Ĝ² + 8αV̂). These functions encode the flattening mechanism.

Linearize R² with an auxiliary scalar, introduce ρ² = ϕ² + G(h), solve the connection equation, and transform with Ω² = ρ²/MPl². The remaining ρ has an algebraic constraint and is integrated out to obtain a K-essence action.

Use the K-inflation background equations, sound speed and Hubble/sound-flow expansion to obtain scalar and tensor spectra. For the worked example, apply the approximately canonical slow-roll limit and express observables in terms of e-fold number and the couplings.

The spectral analysis uses a real symmetric tridiagonal mass matrix, real orthogonal diagonalisation, finite matrix sections and Gershgorin disks. The displayed eigenvalue-size estimate is λ(k)≲|C̄k C̄k+1|, rather than an exact spectrum.

On proportional flat backgrounds, the field equations reduce to successive cubic equations for neighbouring scale ratios. The author invokes Cardano–Tartaglia solutions; setting β2=β3=0 gives an illustrative linear system.

Expansion around the proportional background includes canonical normalisation of metric fluctuations, the ΓΓ form of the Einstein–Hilbert action, and extraction of Fierz–Pauli quadratic mass terms and higher interaction vertices.

The radiative example expresses neutrino masses through the one-loop Passarino–Veltman B0 function. A separate phenomenological illustration estimates W-mediated muon radiative decay using heavy-light neutrino mixing.

Systematic SU(2)L tensor contractions and hypercharge assignments organize effective mass operators and their renormalizable tree-level messenger completions, including induced scalar vacuum expectation values.

Mass matrices are treated by biunitary transformations and perturbative seesaw block diagonalization. The flavour analysis also uses determinant and trace invariants and numerical scans of Yukawa parameters.

Microcanonical species counting is compared with a Schwarzschild entropy bound. Separately, zero-mode spectral counting tests partition-function finiteness, while the reviewed emergence calculation sums one-loop scalar-propagator corrections up to the species scale.

Attractor-mechanism techniques reduce extremal black-hole dynamics to a constrained one-dimensional mechanical system. Scalar gradients serve as a proxy for EFT breakdown and define an effective finite black-hole size.

A covariant field-space treatment uses D_t A^I = dot A^I + Γ^I_JK dot φ^J A^K and the background equation D_t dot φ^I + 3H dot φ^I + V^{,I} = 0. Tangent and normal projections distinguish slow longitudinal evolution from large turning.

The review discusses the coupled quadratic action for curvature and entropic fluctuations, its low-energy single-field EFT with imaginary sound speed, and higher correlation functions. It reports agreement between that EFT and numerical calculations in concrete transiently tachyonic models.

Compute defect fusion by gauging in a slab M×I with Dirichlet conditions on both boundaries. Relative cohomology, Lefschetz duality, and shrinking I identify the gauge-field sum with surfaces in H2(M;ZN); gauge normalization supplies 1/N for connected M.

Use one-form SPT classifications and quadratic finite gauge sums. For odd N, p is modulo N, gcd(p,N)=1, and gauging sends p to −1/(4p), requiring 4p² = −1 mod N. For even N, Pontryagin-square actions require p² = −1 mod 2N bosonically, or mod N fermionically.

Couple the theory in one region to discrete BF gauge theory, with action iN/(2π) times b∧da, and impose a|M = 0 at the interface. Flatness of a supplies the argument that this Dirichlet interface is topological.

Derive fusion through continuum Chern-Simons path integrals and the equivalence of the double-semion theory to twisted Z2 Dijkgraaf-Witten gauge theory. Poincaré duality converts the sum over one-cocycles into surfaces; a gauge-field shift produces the framing sign in surface absorption.

Fix normalization by gauging in a tubular neighborhood M3×I with Dirichlet boundaries. Relative cohomology reduces degree by one; the stated transgression Φ(P(b)) = 2a∪a∪a mod 4 produces the twisted surface condensate and its 1/|H0(M3,Z2)| factor.

Use anomaly inflow to identify the failure of the original zero-form defect after gauging the one-form symmetry. Dress it with an anomaly-cancelling three-dimensional TQFT, choosing the minimal A2,1 = U(1)2 theory; the cited factorization result separates any additional neutral TQFT.

Cosmic-string spectra integrate loop formation, dilution, emission and harmonic contributions. Network evolution uses velocity-dependent one-scale equations rather than instantaneous constant efficiencies.

Uses Friedmann scaling and tensor horizon re-entry/transfer functions for analytic GW spectra; numerically integrates coupled radial, angular and Friedmann equations for homogeneous scalar trajectories.

Construct a generalized Scherk–Schwarz twist and scale factor in SO(8,4) exceptional field theory, impose its consistency conditions, and extract six-dimensional fields using the supergravity dictionary. The authors report that the uplifted family satisfies the six-dimensional equations of motion.

Apply outer automorphisms of SO(4,4) to sphere-reduction twist matrices and embedding tensors. The resulting quarter-maximal theories are equivalent before embedding into SO(8,4), while the embeddings produce inequivalent half-maximal theories.

Find scalar-potential extrema and evaluate dressed embedding-tensor mass matrices. For higher KK levels, expand ExFT fluctuations in round-sphere scalar harmonics transforming as (n/2,n/2) of SO(4), then organize physical modes into supermultiplets after removing absorbed modes.

Impose st crossing on the coefficient expansion, eliminate subtraction-function coefficients where relevant, and convert the resulting homogeneous equalities into null dispersive integrals. These integrals can enter optimization without changing its coefficient objective.

Use dual tensors to impose matrix positivity for every dispersive scale and partial wave. Setting x=µ/Λ²−1 and clearing positive denominators gives a polynomial matrix program for SDPB; complex Hermitian constraints admit a doubled real representation.

Twice-subtracted su dispersion relations use Cauchy's formula and the Froissart–Martin bound. Partial-wave expansion and the generalized optical theorem express coefficient sum rules as integrals over UV-state amplitude products.

Five losses address the Monge–Ampère equation, Kähler closure, patch transitions, Ricci curvature and reference volume. Direct Ricci loss is disabled by default; the potential model also disables closure and volume losses because of its construction.

Compare five ansätze: a free metric network; additive corrections to g_FS; element-wise multiplicative corrections; matrix-product corrections; and a scalar-potential model g_pr=g_FS+∂∂̄φ. The reference g_FS is the pulled-back Fubini–Study metric.

Sample points using complex-geometric results and known ambient-space measures, avoiding MCMC. Monte Carlo integrals use weights w_i=(dVol_CY/dA)|p_i to convert the sampling measure dA into the Calabi–Yau volume measure.

Use the extremal-functional method to estimate long-multiplet dimensions from functional zeros, assuming the limiting bound identifies conformal matter. Functional values on short multiplets also provide conditional evidence for vanishing OPE coefficients.

Search derivative linear functionals normalized on D[2]_adj, nonnegative on other nonidentity contributions, and maximizing the identity functional. The resulting SDP bounds the moment-map OPE coefficient from above and C_J from below.

Decompose the moment-map four-point function into flavor projectors and superconformal blocks. Crossing and the superconformal Ward identity reduce the constraints to one independent sum rule per flavor channel.

Compute toric-divisor Hodge diamonds using cohomCalg's Koszul extension and HodgeDiamond module. When that module fails, obtain h^{1,0} and h^{2,0} from trivial-line-bundle cohomology via a Koszul sequence, then infer h^{1,1} using the divisor Euler characteristic and Hodge dualities.

Construct homogeneous definite-parity generators using integer kernels of weight-difference matrices. Test fixed loci modulo toric C* equivalences through congruence/Diophantine systems; impose generator consistency and SR constraints, then use sector-wise Gröbner-basis ideal dimensions to test hypersurface intersection and reduce redundant generators.

Enumerate disjoint exchanges of NIDs: equal divisor Hodge data but distinct toric charges. Require invariance of the Stanley–Reisner and linear ideals for a proper exchange, preserving the graded Chow ring and triple intersections. Determine h^{1,1}_± from the induced action on independent divisor classes, respecting linear relations.

Write the horizon equation as a cubic in x=rH² and impose nonnegative discriminant as the classical Cosmic Censorship condition. Compare spherical and flat transverse geometries through their different cubic coefficients.

Combine emission kinematics, charge conservation and preservation of censorship with the slope of the extremality curve. Translate the resulting charge-parameter constraint through the holographic chemical potential, horizon-volume enthalpy density and colour-number dictionary.

Use Gauss' law to identify physical charge and integrate dM=T dS at fixed charge to identify the mass parameter. The integration constant is set to zero using Extremal Instability: the author excludes an absolutely stable, electrically neutral, zero-temperature black hole.

Near the inflection point, compare semiclassical Coleman–de Luccia and Hawking–Moss vacuum-transition exponents with the charged Nariai black-hole discharge exponent. The appendix estimates when the Higgs vacuum lasts long enough for the FL argument.

Apply the electron FL inequality to the effective Higgs vacuum energy or total inflationary energy. Relate inflationary energy to the maximum instantaneous reheating temperature and, for single-field slow-roll inflation, relate Hubble scale to the tensor-to-scalar ratio.

Expand the running quartic logarithmically near a fiducial Higgs value, usually its zero h0, and add a stabilizing dimension-six operator. Impose stationary-point and vacuum-energy conditions to estimate UV vacuum and cutoff scales.

Use the Iyer-Wald symplectic current, Noether charge and constraint identity, integrated over a Cauchy surface bounded by infinity and the bifurcation surface. Higher-derivative effects enter as perturbations of the constraints rather than explicit higher-derivative contributions to the horizon entropy term.

Vary correction operators to obtain stress-tensor and electromagnetic-source perturbations, then evaluate their effective-stress integral on the uncorrected solution. The applications examine both local energy-condition contractions and their integral over the spacelike Cauchy surface.

Gauge invariant functional renormalization, equivalently physical gauge fixing with β=−1 and α→0, separates transverse-traceless tensor and physical scalar fluctuations from the gauge/ghost measure sector. The measure contribution is independent of physical-sector couplings.

Numerical simultaneous zeros of four nonlinear beta functions identify the selected R-fixed point. Restricted Einstein–Hilbert and R² truncations are evaluated in the same regulator scheme to assess its identification and truncation dependence.

Projected and off-diagonal heat-kernel expansions evaluate traces through quadratic curvature order on geometries beyond Einstein spaces, retaining tensor–scalar mixing needed to distinguish higher derivative couplings.

Apply Wald entropy directly to the manifestly diffeomorphism-invariant axidilaton action. Gauss-Codazzi relations reduce the stationary Gauss-Bonnet contribution to intrinsic horizon curvature. Check the resulting thermodynamics against δM = TδS + ΩδJ.

Dualize the three-form perturbatively using a Lagrange multiplier for its Bianchi identity, conformally transform to the modified Einstein frame, integrate by parts and remove terms proportional to leading equations of motion through field redefinitions.

Use a corrected Kerr ansatz with four functions Hi, expanded in χ; coefficients are polynomials in 1/ρ and cosθ. Fix integration constants by asymptotic flatness and by requiring M and J to remain physical mass and angular momentum. The solution was computed through χ^40.

De Sitter Bogoliubov coefficients specify squeezing and phase, yielding C_dS=tanh(r)e^(2iΦ). Fixing Λ makes this coefficient independent of the comoving mode label and defines the planar state family.

The square root of the rescaled Fisher quantity is interpreted as an energy uncertainty. Its induced first-order frequency-squared correction is matched to the correction produced by the δ-parametrized quasi-de Sitter background.
The planar Fisher quantity is defined as the variance of a physical-momentum dilation generator and numerically evaluated as a phase-derivative variance, truncating the pair-number sum at N.

Integrate gravitational-wave fluctuations up to momentum cutoff μ on an approximately de Sitter background. Use the Cotton tensor and Einstein equations to organize axion–gravity energy exchange and determine the combined vacuum equation of state.

The appendix treats massless contorted QED by imposing torsion-charge conservation through a path-integral constraint and integrating out nonpropagating torsion. The resulting description contains an axion and fixed-sign repulsive axial-current four-fermion interactions.

Implement the modified Bianchi identity as a delta-functional constraint, introduce a pseudoscalar Lagrange multiplier and perform the quadratic H-field path integral. This yields a canonically normalized dynamical axion with gravitational Chern–Simons coupling.
Compute first at fixed couplings and average afterward; this preserves the distinction between quantum fluctuations within a theory and classical variation between theories.
Insert complete α-state bases between boundary operators and use their common eigenvalue equations to collapse the intermediate sums.
Prepare the thermal boundary geometry and estimate the number of observations needed to resolve a specified microscopic state space. The paper uses an imported quadratic sampling cost.

Distribution reconstruction depends on the measurement algebra. Sector access can reveal individual coupling labels, whereas collective access supplies selected moments and may leave distinct coupling distributions observationally indistinguishable.
Keep the local field content fixed, vary coupling-setting brane separations, and replicate the construction in unused transverse directions.
Choose an elliptic fibration and place D3 probes at base points whose j-invariants realize desired coupling classes.
Replicate each thermal sector, project spectators onto ground states, sum the replica operators over sectors, and divide the trace by K.
Vary compactification moduli geometrically, realize the family as a higher-dimensional noncompact space, and choose the number of localized sectors at each parameter value.

Solve an observable equation for a background combination, substitute each root into a constraint, and test admissibility in the original model. The paper performs the first two operations; n020 reconstructs the omitted domain checks.
This is a symbolic reconstruction and dimensional check of the supplied expressions. It separates an exact background identity from the perturbative status of the adopted observable formulas.

Differentiate the chosen Hubble function, integrate its associated scalar flows, and obtain the potential from the Friedmann constraint. In this application a linear Hubble function reduces the integrations to constant-velocity trajectories.

Differentiate the full potential before restricting it to the trajectory, then test a one-field limit and invariance under orthogonal field-coordinate changes. These checks use the starting field-space expression rather than only a reduced branch formula.

Evaluate branch boundary functions while varying one Hubble-function coefficient and holding other quantities at positive unit values. The source uses these scans to discuss parameter ranges and qualitative observational compatibility.

The audit checks roots against the full starting observable and Hubble equations, not just their reduced threshold expressions. It also distinguishes varying A during inversion from varying an observable at fixed underlying slopes.

Evaluate background kinetic quantities, use the stated horizon-crossing amplitude, differentiate the evolving slow-roll parameter, and infer the tensor ratio. These are the formulas used by the paper, with their perturbative and multifield assumptions left largely implicit.

Extremize the potential with respect to the relaxon, using its dominant dependence through |wX|². For φ-independent relevant Kähler coefficients, extremization can be performed directly with respect to wX; the paper then argues that the leading scaling survives more general φ dependence.

Constrained-superfield EFT: X²=0 describes the goldstino; constraints on Φ remove its independent fermion and auxiliary components. Consequently the auxiliary-field sums in the scalar potential run over T and X, excluding Φ.
Use RG-resummed logarithmic couplings for dilaton stabilization, Weyl transformations for matter couplings, and homogeneous Friedmann/axio-dilaton equations for preliminary cosmological evolution.

RL changes one B integer by ±1 and a C integer in the same row by the same amount, preserving c1(V)=0. Rewards use score improvement, step/boundary penalties and a terminal bonus. REINFORCE and actor–critic use fully connected networks, typically width 64 and depth four.

A shared score combines the family index, anomaly/Mori-cone condition, empty monad degeneracy locus, avoidance of structure-group splitting and trivial summands, index-divisibility tests for equivariance, and basic Hoppe stability checks involving B,C and their duals.

GA fitness equals the same score. The bi-cubic runs use population 250, rank-weighted selection, single-cut crossover and mutation rate 0.004. Independent Mathematica and Python GA implementations connect to the same Mathematica environment.
Use conserved geodesic energy and angular momentum to obtain a one-dimensional effective potential after introducing y = (r/R)^{(1+3w)/(1+w)}.

Linearize the Einstein–fluid equations. Radial modes with time dependence e^{iωt} reduce to a Bessel-type equation; static parity-even tidal perturbations use Regge–Wheeler gauge, interior power laws and exterior associated Legendre functions.

Solve the Tolman–Oppenheimer–Volkoff equations for the prescribed density ansatz; use Israel junction conditions to determine the confining surface stress tensor and calculate the discontinuity in surface gravity.

Modified GRChombo performs fully nonlinear 3+1 numerical-relativity evolution using the BSSN formulation and the scalar Klein–Gordon equation. The spatial metric, extrinsic curvature and scalar momentum are evolved together.

The initial Hamiltonian constraint is solved by relaxing the conformal factor χ from χ=1 through ∂tχ=ℋ until convergence. The specified initial scalar velocity and extrinsic-curvature data satisfy the momentum constraints.

Diagnostics follow scalar settling, the sign and evolution of K, and bubble-wall locations and widths in comoving coordinates. Approximately frozen wall positions are interpreted as expansion with the background.

Begin with a twice-subtracted dispersion relation at t<0. The graviton t-channel pole is recovered from nonuniform convergence of the ultraviolet integral as t→0. Subtracting an asymptotic Regge contribution exposes the pole and permits a reorganized relation near the forward limit.

Define the reduced amplitude Ã=lim(MPl→∞) MPl²A. Graviton loops enter at higher inverse-Planck order and are projected out. The corresponding unitarity relation sums over intermediate states excluding gravitons and supplies elastic positivity.

Construct normalized indefinite photon/graviton helicity states and impose elastic final-state conjugation. Combine definite-helicity amplitudes before subtracting all channel poles. Improved positivity bounds subtract known low-energy loops to test proposed cancellations.

Group embeddings and branching rules, centralizers of Higgs expectation values, exponential maps, and lifting through Spin(10)→SO(10) organize the symmetry-breaking web. Higgs quadratic coefficients and a bias h parameterize the proposed phase diagram.

Anomaly inflow and cobordism constrain allowed phases; electric centers and Pontryagin duals of fundamental groups organize 1-form symmetries. Fusion of flip-invariant magnetic surface operators tests non-invertibility.

Use local toric intersections and divisor linear equivalences to determine cubic self-intersections, then integrated Chern classes and volumes. Superimposing Bianchi identities across triangulations amounts to separating coefficients of the triangulation-dependent functions.

Evaluate a representation-dependent multiplicity operator and decompose it into local contributions. An all-S reference configuration plus local difference operators describes spectral changes. Kähler-volume expressions also enter the loop-corrected Donaldson–Uhlenbeck–Yau equations.

Introduce indicator functions δ^T_αβγ, equal to one for the chosen triangulation and zero otherwise, with ΣTδ^T=1. Three combinations Δi encode local choices; for example Δ1=−δ^E1+δ^E2+δ^E3. These parameterise intersection numbers without enumerating global configurations.

Bayesian MCMC estimates marginal posterior distributions for α, n and ω using a likelihood proportional to exp(−χ²/2). Reported parameter errors are 1σ, or 68%; contour plots are described as showing 68% and 95% confidence regions.

The Hubble likelihood uses a sum of squared Hth−Hobs residuals divided by observational variances. The supernova likelihood uses distance-modulus residuals and the Pantheon covariance matrix, with DL=(1+z)c∫0^z dẑ/H(ẑ) and μth=5log10[DL/(10 pc)].
